results.summary: This project implements a 4x4 multiplier in structural Verilog, producing an 8-bit product from two 4-bit inputs. It is built from an array of full adders that combine partial products, following a classic textbook multiplier structure. The design is intended as a lab exercise and is tested by applying input pairs and comparing the output to the expected product. No external hardware is required, and the documentation is sufficient to understand the basic operation.

This design is a 4x4 array multiplier that computes the product of two 4-bit binary numbers using full adders. It was created as a lab exercise to demonstrate binary multiplication and the role of full adders in digital circuits. Testing involves applying various input combinations and comparing the output to the expected product. No external hardware is needed, and the documentation provides a clear explanation of the design and test procedure.

This project is a 4-bit multiplier that multiplies two 4-bit binary numbers using full adders to produce an 8-bit product. It is tested by specifying two 4-bit inputs in a Python test script and verifying the output against the expected product. The design requires no external hardware. The documentation is brief but sufficient to describe the function and testing method.

This is a 4x4 array multiplier implemented in Verilog that multiplies two 4-bit numbers to produce an 8-bit product. The design is based on a standard array multiplier structure using full adders. Testing is performed by adding test cases in a Python script and following the instructions in the test README. No external hardware is required, and the documentation is minimal but adequate.

This project implements a 4-bit multiplier that takes two 4-bit inputs and produces an 8-bit product using full adders. The inputs are split into two 4-bit portions, and the multiplication is performed through adder logic. Testing is done using a testbench with idle cases. No external hardware is needed, but the documentation is very sparse and lacks detail on the exact implementation and test procedure.

This design is an 8-bit carry-skip adder that adds two 8-bit numbers using a combination of ripple-carry and skip logic to reduce carry propagation delay. The adder is divided into two 4-bit sections, and the final sum is registered and output synchronously with the clock. Testing involves applying input values to the ui_in and uio_in pins and verifying the sum on uo_out after each clock edge. No external hardware is required, and the documentation provides a clear explanation of the operation and test method.

This project implements an 8-bit carry-skip adder that adds two 8-bit numbers using ripple-carry and skip logic for improved performance. The design splits the addition into two 4-bit sections and registers the output in sync with the clock. Testing is done by applying inputs to ui_in and uio_in and checking the sum on uo_out after each rising edge. No external hardware is needed, and the documentation is identical to another project, suggesting it may be a duplicate or shared design.

This project is a tiny encryption core that takes a 4-bit input and a 4-bit key to produce a 4-bit encrypted output. It is intended to be tested by sending randomized 4-bit inputs and keys and observing the output. The design requires no external hardware, though memory may be needed to supply test data. The documentation is very limited, providing only a high-level description without details on the encryption algorithm or test methodology.

This design is a VGA demo that displays an image of a plane flying into the sunset with text overlaid. It runs automatically and outputs VGA signals on the uo pins, requiring a VGA PMOD connected to the output. The project is a re-run of a previous demo and mentions an unsuccessful attempt at a clock domain crossing project. The documentation is minimal, focusing on the visual output rather than technical details.

This project implements a Hopfield neural network on-chip using Izhikevich-type regular spiking and fast spiking neurons with on-chip Hebbian learning for pattern storage and retrieval. It accepts a learning enable signal and a 4-bit pattern input, and outputs spikes from seven neurons via bidirectional pins. The design is a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron model and is intended to be tested, though the documentation provides little detail on the test procedure. No external hardware is required, but the documentation is sparse and lacks specifics on operation and verification.
